lines.note: Hissui no kotowari completes shōsha hissui from f198, the principle that flourishing is followed by decline. The prior page's isolated hissui is therefore a catchword.

runs.text: & proſperão mas logo desfalecem, ou deſcaẽ.

lines.note: Those who prosper soon weaken or decline. Desfalecem is one verb here, not des followed by a separate word.
Hisukashina describes an irascible, harsh person. Peſſoa is badly worn but its role and remaining types support the restoration.

runs.text: Hum paſſarinho aſſi chamado de varias

lines.note: Hisui is a small multicoloured bird, recognizably the kingfisher sense. The gloss itself supplies no further species distinction.
Cores completes varias cores, the bird's varied colours. The isolated word is a normal body continuation.
Hisui no kanzashi is a head or hair ornament. The preceding bird entry offers context, but the gloss does not explicitly state its material.

runs.text: cabeça, ou cabelos de molheres nobres.

lines.note: The ornament is worn by noblewomen. Preserve molheres, the period spelling, rather than introduce a modern vowel.
Hita is a clapper or other bird-scaring device, explained as a kind of naruko. The scan has tagvi, using v in the internal vowel position; the reading is tagui (a kind), not a different lexical item.

runs.text: ra eſpantar os paſſaros, & outros animaes das

lines.note: Its purpose is frightening birds and other animals away. Pe-ra connects the purpose clause across the physical line.
Searas specifies the crops or fields being protected. This closes the clapper's agricultural definition.
Hitaka is glossed as a kestrel-like falcon. The damaged F is resolved without assuming an exact modern species equivalence.
Hitakabuto denotes armed soldiers. Kabuto evokes armour, while the Portuguese explicitly refers to the people wearing it.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de chegarſe, ou de

lines.note: Hitahita to means close contact or adherence here. The repeated fita pattern restores the garbled Firancato.

runs.text: eſtar pegado, ou afferrado a algũa couſa.

lines.note: Being pressed against or attached to something completes the adverb's explanation. Algũa repairs the damaged generic object phrase.
Hitai is the forehead. The visible t and direct teſta gloss correct OCR's Ficai.
Hitaigami refers to children's long forehead hair. The compound uses the hitai just defined, not a separate hik- stem.
Testa completes the hair-location phrase. The short continuation should retain its own crop and ID.

runs.text: Hum ferro que poem os ſoldados na

lines.note: Hitaigane is an iron forehead guard worn by soldiers. The next lines explain its mounting and purpose.

runs.text: testa ſobre algum veo que amarrão na cabeça

lines.note: It sits above a cloth tied around the head. ſobre repairs the OCR j while preserving veo as printed.
The guard receives or stops arrows. Frechas is retained as the period Portuguese form.

runs.text: O atormentar, ou por em aperto ſem

lines.note: Hitazeme means unremitting pressure or assault. The citation spelling Fitajeme is supported by the scan despite modern zeme expectations.
Shiro wo hitazeme ni semuru applies the expression to besieging a castle. The repeated fitajeme repairs the draft's ficajeme.

runs.text: Ter de cerco a fortaleza combatendoa rijamen

lines.note: The fortress is kept under siege and attacked vigorously. Rijamen continues into rijamente below.
The attack proceeds without stopping. This completes the incessant-assault definition.
Hitamono is an adverb meaning greatly and continually. Continuada- is a single printed word before its ending on the next line.
Sore ni yotte introduces the result in a Christian example. Chriſtão is in the Japanese quotation and is not a new Portuguese gloss here.
Hitamono ni hanjō tsukamatsuru describes continual flourishing. Mon is the citation label; the o mark in fanjǒ is visibly present.

runs.text: iſſo a Chriſtãodade não fazia ſe não crecer, &

lines.note: Por iſſo says that consequently Christianity kept growing. The badly damaged OCR phrase is restored from the scan, not paraphrased into modern Portuguese.
Dilatarſe completes growth and expansion. It remains part of the Christian example's translation.
Hitan is sorrow or lament, explained as kanashimi and nageku. The scan resolves both the headword's final n and the missing n in Canaximi.
Afligirſe adds distress to becoming sorrowful. This closes the emotional rather than physical meaning.
Hitaru is soaking or immersing oneself deeply. The final mui is divided from muito, not a Japanese particle.

runs.text: to na agoa, ou noutra couſa liquida.

lines.note: Water or another liquid is the medium. The alternatives define immersion broadly rather than restrict it to water.
Hitasawagi ni describes sustained agitation. Fitaſauaguini is recoverable from the scan and its repetition below.
People can become greatly and continually agitated. Aluoraçar muito restores the lost vowel and word division in the OCR.
The agitation also applies to animals. Hitasawagi ni sa-wagu is the Japanese example; animais corrects the draft's aximais.
Wagu completes sawagu, making a commotion. The split occurs inside the Japanese verb.
Hitasura or hitasura ni describes persistent entreaty. The visible long-s forms restore the garbled headword and repeated alternative.
Gar completes rogar, asking humbly and importunately. The initial is not a capital B or an independent word.

runs.text: Hum vestido que vſão os Cũgues, &

lines.note: Hitatare is a garment worn by court nobles and soldiers. The clothing gloss and scan resolve the damaged headword and veſtido.
Soldiers wear it over armour. ſoldados and armas repair letter errors without changing the claim about how the garment is worn.
Hitato is equated with hitahita to. The repeated adverb confirms close contact, not the OCR's Cataxo.

runs.text: eſtar pegado, ou de estar continuamente junto,

lines.note: The sense is staying attached or continuously close. Eſtar pegado restores the garbled beginning of the Portuguese clause.
Aferrado adds being fastened or firmly attached. This completes the cluster of contact expressions.
Hitauchi is repeated striking without intervals. Fi begins the identical example word on the next line.
Hitauchi ni utsu is beating continuously. The scan's tauchini replaces the entirely misread quemini.
Sem deſcanſar completes the uninterrupted action. It is body text and must not be mistaken for a footer.
Hitasu means soaking or thoroughly wetting something. Vt introduces an example, not Vide pointing to another entry.

runs.text: Yamabato ſuxẽ tõbi qitatte tçubaſauo miz

lines.note: Thousands of mountain pigeons fly up and wet their wings. Su-xẽ and tõbi preserve nasal abbreviations; miz begins the word for water below.

Zuni completes mizzu ni, in water, followed by hitaite. Taif is the source label and Lib. 29 its reference. Even in the enlargement no secure s can be restored in fitaite: retain the anomalous printed reading, although hitashite is expected from the verb and meaning.

runs.text: do voando milhares de pombos trocazes banha

lines.note: The Portuguese describes thousands of wood pigeons coming in flight. Banha continues the bathing verb on the next line.
They bathe their wings in water. Umi, kumo wo hi-tasu then introduces a different example of sea waves reaching clouds.

runs.text: Chegarem as ondas às nuuẽs como ba-

lines.note: Taſu completes hitasu, not tatu. The waves seem to touch or wet the clouds, matching the Japanese image.
The appearance is described as seen from afar. The dictionary qualifies the image rather than claiming literal clouds are submerged.
Hitba, a Sino-Japanese horse term, is equated with uma. The consonant cluster includes b, not OCR's h.
Hitbarasō names a Siamese herb. The gloss does not support a more precise botanical identification in Level 1.
Hitboku is fude and sumi, brush and ink. The Chinese-compound ending boku is directly supported by the explanatory Japanese.
Hitsu is a chest or box. Caixão is not restricted here to its modern coffin sense.
Hitsuchigome or hitsuchi no kome is a second rice growth. The damaged initial letters are resolved by the repeated hitsuchi and the NINJAL headword.

runs.text: roz que vem, ou nace a ſegunda vez de pois

lines.note: The rice grows a second time after the first harvest. ſegunda is the ordinal, not an f-initial word.
De ſegado o primeiro completes the condition: the first crop has been cut. This is regrowth, not simply a second sowing stated by the text.
Hitsuji denotes sheep. The following homonym uses the same zodiac animal for a time designation.

runs.text: Nome de hũa das horas de Iapão que

lines.note: Hitsuji also names a Japanese hour after midday. Its time sense must be kept separate from the animal definition.
Hitsuji ni naru means reaching that hour. The damaged ni was misread as ri; the following alternative confirms the construction.
Hitsuji no toki de gozaru is the alternative time expression. The Portuguese gives one to two after midday, with tè functioning as until.

runs.text: duas de pois de meo dia pouco mais, ou menos.

lines.note: Pouco mais ou menos qualifies the approximate hour. It repairs two clear OCR errors without imposing a modern exact time conversion.
Hitsuji-saru names a compass direction between the zodiac positions. The Portuguese correspondence follows below.
Ao Sudueste identifies southwest. Ao is the required preposition and is visible, not the draft's do.
Hitdai points to Fiddai, an alternative spelling. Preserve both forms instead of regularizing the gemination across references.
Hitdō is fude no michi, the art of writing. The literal brush-way paraphrase establishes the calligraphic meaning.
Hitjō, written Fitgiǒ, is kanarazu sadamaru, certainly determined. Its gi spelling remains distinct from gui in the next entry.
Certa and aueriguada complete the assured or established quality. This is the certainty entry, not the brush-form entry below.
Fitguiǒ is fude no katachi, the form of the writing brush. Gui and gi cannot be conflated merely because the neighboring headwords look similar.

runs.text: de eſcreuer letra de Iapão. ( S.

lines.note: The brush is used for Japanese letters. The far-right ( S. is physically preserved here; its marker warns that logical attachment may differ from this row's main gloss.
Hitzen means certainly, glossed kanarazu. Its checked-final-t spelling Fitjen is not expanded into modern syllables in Level 1.
Hitzetsu combines brush and tongue, with bunshō as the explanatory term. The visible i is an explanation marker rather than a capital Japanese initial.
Fitjet ni tsukushi-gatashi begins an expression of being impossible to exhaust in words or writing. Falar repairs the draft's fatar.

runs.text: Não ſe pode eſplicar por pena, ou

lines.note: Gatashi completes the difficulty construction. The Portuguese says it cannot be explained by pen or writing.
Eſcrito completes that gloss, followed by S. The extra apparent a is an ink blemish, not a transcribed word.
Hitmetsu is inevitable destruction, kanarazu messuru. The damaged citation form is Fitmet, preserving its checked codas.
Shōja hitmetsu says those born inevitably perish. This Buddhist maxim explains the general destruction sense.
The Portuguese states that those born unfailingly end. Feiq is the source label; the scan shows book 4, not the OCR's pilcrow.
Hitō, akai momo, is the red-peach blossom sense. Its marked o distinguishes it from hito, person, below.
Vermelha completes the blossom's intense red colour. It agrees with flor rather than implying the whole tree is red.
Hito includes either a man or woman. The broad human meaning is explicit rather than inferred from a masculine Portuguese noun alone.
Hitoai is equated with nin-ai, human interaction or sociability. The i is explanatory, not an alternative-conjunction l.
Pedro wa hitoai ga yoi means Pedro is pleasant in his dealings. Pedroua corrects the draft's Podroua while preserving the fused particle.

runs.text: bom modo em tratar, & conuerſar, ou he a-

lines.note: He has good manners in dealing and conversation. A begins apraziuel across the line break.
Praziuel completes pleasant or agreeable in conversation. This closes the sociability example.
Hitoawase is a single encounter. The repeated example begins before the continuation below.
Hitoawase mo seide nigeta hito ja describes someone who fled without even one encounter. Xeide is the negative conjunctive expression in the printed spelling.

runs.text: fugio ſem ter hum ſò encontro com alguem.

lines.note: Fugio ſem ter hum confirms fleeing without having a single encounter. Several OCR substitutions had obscured this straightforward Portuguese clause.
Hitoawase mo awasenu tori ja concerns a cock that cannot be matched even once. The next line gives the bird explicitly, so this is not another human encounter.

runs.text: lo que o não farão encontrar com outro: mas não

lines.note: Galo completes the cock gloss, followed by a warning about an expression that should not be used. The prohibition continues onto f200.
Printed catchword anticipating the opening of f200; verified against that scan. Preserved outside body text with its original stable ID.
